Lichen sclerosus (vulva)

In an uncontrolled study, seven of eight quality-of-life domains improved after ten PBM sessions. The study did not establish whether disease activity, scarring, or long-term symptoms improved because it had no comparison group.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In an uncontrolled study, seven of eight quality-of-life domains improved after ten PBM sessions. The study did not establish whether disease activity, scarring, or long-term symptoms improved because it had no comparison group.

Summary of the Evidence

One prospective observational study examined PBM as an addition to existing treatment for vulvar lichen sclerosus. It enrolled 100 women whose symptoms had not been adequately relieved by topical treatment; 94 completed the ten-session course and follow-up. No controlled PBM trial, duplicate report, animal study, or cell-culture study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

After treatment, seven of eight health-related quality-of-life domains improved significantly. Most DoloTest symptom dimensions also improved, with the smoking-related measure not reaching statistical significance. These are patient-reported changes after a treatment course and are directly relevant to perceived burden. The study did not establish whether clinical disease activity, scarring, or vulvar architecture changed, and its uncontrolled design cannot show that PBM caused the improvements (Berthelsen et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

No animal model study of PBM for vulvar lichen sclerosus was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct laboratory or ex-vivo PBM study of this condition was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The observational study used an 808-nm near-infrared laser at 500 mW for ten sessions over eight weeks. The paper describes PBM as a supplement to topical treatment, so the findings do not support replacing established care. A sham comparison, clear reporting of session duration and delivered fluence, and longer follow-up would help distinguish light effects from symptom fluctuation and concurrent treatment.

Interpretation

Most quality-of-life domains improved among the women who completed treatment. This shows a favorable change in patient-reported burden during the study, while the absence of a control group leaves its cause uncertain. There is not yet evidence that PBM changes the underlying disease or prevents scarring.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for short-term improvement in patient-reported burden
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One prospective observational study found improvement in seven of eight quality-of-life domains among 94 women who completed ten sessions. Without a comparison group, the change cannot be separated from concurrent topical care or symptom fluctuation, and objective disease activity was not established. A sham-controlled trial with validated symptoms, examination measures, and longer follow-up would support a stronger assessment.
